Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 85, verses 1–3:

Meccan, and its verses are 22 [revealed after Surat ash-Shams]. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

It is said: "the constellations" (al-buruj) are the twelve zodiacal signs, and they are "palaces of the sky" by way of metaphor. It was also said: "al-buruj" means the stars that are the stations of the moon (manazil al-qamar). It was also said: the great stars. They were called buruj (from burj, a tower or prominent structure) because of their visibility. It was also said: they are the gates of the sky.

﴿And by the Day promised﴾: the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And by the witness and the witnessed﴾: meaning, a witness on that day and one witnessed on it.

The "witness" is whoever among all creation bears witness on that day, and the "witnessed" is what occurs on that day of its wonders.

As for the reason why both are indefinite (nakira): either it is what you mentioned in His words ﴿A soul will know what it has presented﴾, as if it were said: "by a witness and a witnessed whose abundance is extraordinary." **Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 85, verses 4–9:**

If you ask: where is the answer to the oath? I say: it is omitted, and it is indicated by His words ﴿Cursed were the people of the trench﴾. It is as if it were said: "By these things, they are accursed," meaning the disbelievers of Quraysh, just as the people of the trench were cursed. This is because the surah was revealed to strengthen the believers and to make them patient under the harm of the people of Makkah, and to remind them of what happened to those before them: torture for their faith, the infliction of various kinds of harm, and their patience and steadfastness, so that they would find comfort in them and be patient with what they suffered from their people, and know that their disbelievers, in the sight of God, are in the same position as those tormented and burned with fire, accursed and worthy of being said of them: "Quraysh is cursed," just as it was said: "The people of the trench were cursed." "Qutila" (was cursed) is a supplication against them, like His words ﴿Cursed is man! How ungrateful he is!﴾. It is also recited as "quttila," with the doubled letter.

Al-ukhdud (the trench): a cut or furrow in the earth, which is a split. Similar to it in form and meaning are "al-khaqq" and "al-akhquq." From the same root is the saying: "Its legs sank into the holes of the jerboas." [The commentator's note: in al-Sihah (the lexicon), "al-jurdh" is a type of mouse, and its plural is "al-jurdhan."]

It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: There was a sorcerer for one of the kings. When he grew old, he sent a boy to him to teach him sorcery. On the boy's path was a monk, and he listened to him. One day, on his way, he saw an animal that had blocked the people. He took a stone and said: "O God, if the monk is dearer to You than the sorcerer, then kill it." It was killed. From then on, the boy would heal the blind and the leper and cure other ailments. A companion of the king who had gone blind was healed by him, and the king saw him and asked him: "Who restored your sight?" He said: "My Lord." The king became angry and tortured him, until he pointed to the boy, and the boy was tortured until he pointed to the monk. The monk did not give up his religion, so he was split with a saw. The boy was brought to a mountain to be thrown from its peak. He prayed, and the mountain shook with the people, and they fell, and he was saved. Then he was taken to a boat, and they boarded with him to drown him. He prayed, and the boat capsized with them, and they drowned, and he was saved. Then he said to the king: "You cannot kill me until you gather the people in an open ground, crucify me on a trunk, take an arrow from my quiver, and say: 'In the name of God, the Lord of the boy,' then shoot me with it." He shot him, and it struck his temple, and he placed his hand on it and died. The people said: "We believe in the Lord of the boy." It was said to the king: "What you were afraid of has happened." So he ordered trenches to be dug at the mouths of the streets, and fires were lit in them, and whoever did not return (to disbelief) was thrown into them, until a woman came with a child, and she hesitated to throw herself into it. The child said: "O mother, be patient, for you are upon the truth," so she plunged in. It was also said: he said to her: "Hold back and do not hesitate." It was also said: he said to her: "It is only a brief moment," so she was patient.

[Note: Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Hibban, al-Tabari, al-Tabarani, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Ya'la, and al-Bazzar all narrated it through Ibn Abi Layla in various chains; the version closest to the wording of the text is that of al-Tabari. It was narrated uniquely by Thabit al-Bunani from Abd al-Rahman.]

And from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him): when they differed about the rulings concerning the Magians, he said: "They are people of a scripture, and they adhered to their scripture. Wine had been made lawful for them, and one of their kings drank it and became intoxicated, and he had intercourse with his sister. When he sobered up, he regretted it and sought a way out. His sister said to him: 'The way out is that you address the people and say: O people, God has permitted the marriage of sisters.' Then you address them again and say: 'God has forbidden it.'" He addressed them, but they did not accept it from him. She said: "Lash them with the whip," but they did not accept it. She said: "Strike them with the sword," but they did not accept it. So she ordered trenches, the lighting of fires, and the throwing into them of whoever refused. These are the ones whom God meant by His words ﴿the people of the trench were cursed﴾.

[Note: Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Abu Ya'la, al-Tabari, al-Tabarani, Ahmad, Ishaq, and al-Bazzar all narrated it through Abd al-Rahman ibn Humayd. Al-Tabari narrated it through Ja'far ibn Abi al-Mughira from Abd al-Rahman ibn Ayza, who said: "When the Muslims defeated the people of al-Isfidhiyan and withdrew, Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) came to them, and they gathered and said: 'What rulings apply to the Magians?' He said: 'They are not people of a scripture, nor are they among the polytheist Arabs.' They said: 'They are people of a scripture,' and then he related it. Al-Tabari's version is more complete.]

And it was said: a man from among those who followed the religion of Jesus (peace be upon him) came to Najran, and he invited them, and they responded to him. Then Dhu Nuwas the Jew marched against them with troops from Himyar. He gave them the choice between the fire and Judaism, but they refused, so he burned twelve thousand of them in the trenches. It was also said: seventy thousand.

[Note: Ibn Ishaq narrated it in his Sirah: "Yazid ibn Abi Ziyad related to me from Muhammad ibn Ka'b," and mentioned it at length.]

It is also mentioned that the length of the trench was forty cubits and its width twelve cubits.

[Note: al-Tha'labi narrated it from al-Kalbi.]

And it is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that whenever he mentioned the people of the trench, he sought refuge from the severity of the calamity.

[Note: Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated it from Abu Usama, from Awf, from al-Hasan, with this wording.]

﴿The fire﴾ is a substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal, a grammatical term meaning a noun that is a part of the preceding noun in a broader sense) for ﴿the trench﴾. ﴿Full of fuel﴾ is a description of it, meaning that it is a great fire, having a great quantity of firewood that its flames rise with, and human bodies. It is also recited "al-wuqud" with a damma. ﴿When﴾ is an adverb governing ﴿was cursed﴾, meaning: they were cursed when they surrounded the fire, sitting around it. The meaning of ﴿upon it﴾ is upon what is near it from the edges of the trench, as in the line:

"The dew and the guest spent the night by the fire."

[Note: The explanation of this line was given earlier in the third part, page 53; refer to it if you wish.]

Just as you say: "He passed by him," meaning: while being above a place near him. The meaning of their witnessing the burning of the believers is that they were appointed to that and made witnesses, so that some of them would testify for others before the king that none of them had neglected what he had been commanded and entrusted with regarding the torture. It is also permissible to mean that they are witnesses to what they do to the believers, and they will give their testimony on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿On the Day when their tongues, their hands, and their feet will bear witness against them concerning what they used to do﴾.

﴿And they did not resent from them﴾: they did not find fault with them and did not object to them, except for their faith, as in the line:

"There is no fault in them except that their swords..."

[Note: The explanation of this line was given earlier in the second part, page 142; refer to it if you wish.]

Ibn al-Ruqayyat said:

"They resented nothing from the Banu Umayyah except that they are forbearing when they are angry."

[Note: This is from Qays al-Ruqayyat. "Naqimu" means "they disliked." "Hilm" (forbearance) with the vowel pattern of "zarf" means forgiveness. The poet means that they made the best quality, forbearance when angry, into something ugly. It is also permissible that the subject of both verbs is the pronoun of the Banu Umayyah, and it is permissible that the first belongs to them and the second to those who resent. In it is the sequence of praise with what resembles blame, for the sake of intensifying the praise, since he made forbearance when angry a blame, although it is the utmost in praise. It is also narrated as "ma naqama al-nas," and in that case the correct form is to drop "bayn" for the sake of the meter.]

Abu Haywa recited "naqimu" with a kasra, but the eloquent form is with a fatha.

And He mentioned the attributes by which He deserves to be believed in and worshipped: that He is Mighty, Dominant, Powerful, whose punishment is to be feared, Praiseworthy, Bountiful, to whom praise is due for His blessings, and whose reward is hoped for. ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾. So everyone in them is obligated to worship Him and to submit to Him, by necessity. For what ﴿they resented from them﴾ is the truth, which none resents except a falsifier who is immersed in error. And indeed, those who resent are deserving of God's retribution through a punishment that nothing else equals. ﴿And God is over all things a Witness﴾: a warning to them, meaning that He knows what they did, and He will repay them for it.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 85, verses 12–16:**

*Al-batsh* (the seizing with force): seizing with violence. When it is described as *shadid* (severe), it has been intensified and magnified. It is His seizing of tyrants and oppressors, and His taking them with punishment and retribution. ﴿Indeed, He is the One who originates and repeats﴾, meaning: He originates the seizing and repeats it. That is, He seizes them in this world and in the Hereafter. Or, His power to originate and to bring back indicates the severity of His seizing.

He threatens the disbelievers that He will bring them back as He originated them, in order to seize them, since they did not give thanks for the blessing of origination and they denied the return.

It is also recited as ﴿He originates and repeats﴾, meaning that the One who is *al-Wadud* (the Loving) does to the people of His obedience what the Loving does: giving them what they desire.

It is also recited as ﴿Lord of the Throne﴾ (*dhu al-arsh*) as a description of your Lord. It is also recited as ﴿the Glorious﴾ (*al-majid*) in the genitive, as a description of the Throne. The glory of God (*majd Allah*) is His greatness. The glory of the Throne (*majd al-arsh*) is its elevation and greatness.

﴿Doer of whatever He wills﴾ (*fa'alun*) is the predicate of an omitted subject. It is said *fa'\u0101l* (intensive form) because what He wills and does is extremely abundant.

[[Mahmud said: "It is only said *fa'\u0101l* because what He wills and does is in extreme abundance." Ahmad says: They have not measured God with His due measure. Why did he not say: "There is no doer except Him"? Who opposes that except a polytheist? How many things God willed, according to the opinion of the Qadariyya (the sect who deny divine predestination), He did not do! Suppose we set aside the consideration of the intensive form's emphasis: has He not indicated, by His words ﴿whatever He wills﴾, the generality of His action in all that He wills? So reducing it to the particular is nothing but a retreat from the texts.]]

Pharaoh and Thamud: a substitution for "the hosts."

By Pharaoh he means himself and his household, as in His saying ﴿from Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾. The meaning is: you have come to know the denial of those hosts of the Messengers and what befell them because of their denial.

﴿Rather, those who disbelieve﴾ among your people are ﴿in denial﴾, meaning: in denial and deserving of the punishment. ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of their circumstances and Able over them, and they cannot overcome Him.﴾ ﴿And Allah encompasses them from behind them﴾ is a metaphor, because they cannot escape Him, just as one who flees cannot escape from that which encompasses him.

The sense of the transition (al-idrab, "rather") is that their affair is more remarkable than that of those earlier peoples, because they heard the accounts of those peoples and what happened to them, and they saw the traces of their destruction, yet they did not take heed, and their denial is more severe than theirs.

﴿Rather, it is a glorious Qur'an﴾: that which they denied is a noble Qur'an, lofty in rank among the books, and in its composition and its inimitability.

It was also recited as "Qur'anun Majid" with the genitive construction (bi-l-idafa), meaning: the Qur'an of a glorious Lord.

Yahya ibn Ya'mar recited it as:

﴿in a preserved tablet﴾. "Al-lawh" (the tablet) means "al-hawa'" (the air/space). The Sahih lexicon of al-Jawhari defines "al-lawh" with a damma as the air between the heaven and the earth. [Note (ʿ) as in the original.] That is, the tablet is above the seventh heaven, in which is the preserved tablet, protected from the reach of the devils. It was also recited as "mahfuz" with a raf' (nominative), as an adjective of the Qur'an.

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Buruj, Allah will grant him, for every Friday and every Day of 'Arafah that occurs in this world, ten good deeds." [Reported by al-Wahidi, al-Tha'labi and Ibn Mardawayh with their chains to Ibn Ka'b.]

﴿Rather, it is a glorious Qur'an﴾: that which they denied is a noble Qur'an, lofty in rank among the books, and in its composition and its inimitability.

It was also recited as "Qur'anun Majid" with the genitive construction (bi-l-idafa), meaning: the Qur'an of a glorious Lord.

Yahya ibn Ya'mar recited it as:

﴿in a preserved tablet﴾. "Al-lawh" (the tablet) means "al-hawa'" (the air/space). The Sahih lexicon of al-Jawhari defines "al-lawh" with a damma as the air between the heaven and the earth. [Note (ʿ) as in the original.] That is, the tablet is above the seventh heaven, in which is the preserved tablet, protected from the reach of the devils. It was also recited as "mahfuz" with a raf' (nominative), as an adjective of the Qur'an.

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Buruj, Allah will grant him, for every Friday and every Day of 'Arafah that occurs in this world, ten good deeds." [Reported by al-Wahidi, al-Tha'labi and Ibn Mardawayh with their chains to Ibn Ka'b.]
